turns.doctor_question: Hello. I am Dr. Smith. To get us started, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. Thanks for seeing me. So, um, well, the main thing that really pushed me to finally make an appointment and come in today is work-related. I work as a clerk processing insurance claims and policies—I actually took the job after I left college a few years ago, and it's a decent job, you know, good benefits and everything, but it requires a lot of focused computer work. 

And the problem is, I just keep getting up from my workstation during the day. Like, constantly. I know I’m supposed to stay put. I have these daily quotas and I know I need to just sit in my chair and finish my claim reviews, but I'll be in the middle of reading through a policy, and the next thing I know, I'm up. I'll walk to the breakroom, or I'll go check the mailroom even if I don't have any physical mail to process, or I'll just wander over to the printer even when I haven't printed anything. 

It's not like I don't want to do the work, or that I don't understand the rules of the office. I know exactly what I'm supposed to be doing. I'll even tell myself, "Okay, you are going to sit here and finish this batch of claims," and then ten minutes later I'm out of my seat again. It's incredibly frustrating because I know I need to just sit there and do the work, but I keep abandoning my desk and it's really starting to weigh on me.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they constantly get up from their workstation and abandon their desk despite knowing they are supposed to stay seated to finish their work.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your time in school, did you experience these same difficulties with staying seated or focusing on tasks during class?
turns.patient_response:
You know, it's funny you ask that, because when I really sit down and think about it... no, this definitely isn't a brand new thing for me at all. I was actually just talking to my mom about this a while back when she was cleaning out some old boxes, and she found a bunch of my old report cards from elementary school. 

It was honestly kind of wild reading through the comments sections on those things. Like, almost every single year, my teachers would write these very specific notes. They always started out nice, saying I was a bright kid—which, you know, makes you feel good—but then it was always followed by a "but." It was always, "he's bright, but..." And the "but" was always about how I was constantly losing my worksheets. I mean, I distinctly remember having this crumpled mess of papers shoved into the bottom of my backpack or crammed into the back of my desk, and I could never, ever find the one specific math sheet or spelling list we were supposed to be turning in. 

And they also wrote that I was always missing instructions. Like, the teacher would stand up at the front of the room and explain exactly how to do an assignment, and I’d be looking right at her, but somehow the information just... didn't register. I'd end up having to look around at what the other kids were doing to figure out what step we were on. And the teachers were constantly having to come over to my desk, tap on it, and give me these reminders to actually finish my classwork, because I’d get halfway through a page of problems and then just completely zone out or start staring at the wall. So, yeah, I guess when I really look back at it, this whole struggle to just focus and get the thing done has been trailing me for a really long time.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes zoning out halfway through a page of problems and struggling to maintain focus on tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient notes that even when looking directly at the teacher giving instructions, the information would not register.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient reports failing to finish classwork and needing constant reminders from teachers to complete assignments.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes having a disorganized, crumpled mess of papers shoved into their backpack and desk.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly states they were constantly losing worksheets and could never find the specific papers they needed to turn in.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your elementary school years, besides the difficulties with focus and organization, would you say you were also physically restless, like having trouble staying in your seat or feeling the need to constantly move around?
turns.patient_response:
You know, it's weird, but no, not really. Like, I know I just told you about how I can't stay in my chair at work now, which is why I'm here, but back then? I actually didn't have that problem. I remember my mom always saying I was actually a pretty quiet kid physically. I mean, I wasn't one of those boys who was bouncing off the walls or getting in trouble for running around the classroom when we were supposed to be sitting on the reading rug. 

I'd sit there, you know? I'd be right there in my little plastic chair. It's just that my brain wasn't in the chair with me, if that makes sense. Like, the teachers would be talking about fractions or the Oregon Trail or whatever, and my body was completely stationary, but in my head, I was a million miles away, thinking about a video game or just kind of staring into space at the dust motes floating in the window light. 

There was this one kid in my third-grade class, Tommy, I think his name was, and he was the one who was always jumping up to sharpen his pencil every two minutes or tipping his chair back until he fell over. The teacher was always yelling at him to sit down. But me? I never got yelled at for moving around. I just got those little taps on the desk to wake me up from my daydreams. So, yeah, the physical getting-up-and-walking-around thing I do at the insurance office now... that feels new, or at least, it wasn't something I did when I was little. Back then, I was totally fine just sitting still, even if I wasn't actually getting any of the work done while I was sitting there.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts, stating their brain was 'a million miles away, thinking about a video game or just kind of staring into space.'
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly confirms currently leaving their seat when expected to stay seated, mentioning they 'can't stay in my chair at work now' and 'the physical getting-up-and-walking-around thing I do at the insurance office now.'

turns.doctor_question: When you find yourself getting up from your desk at work now, do you feel an internal sense of jitteriness or physical agitation that forces you to move, or are you just trying to find a way to escape the boredom of the task?
turns.patient_response:
It's definitely more about escaping, but I don't know if "boredom" is exactly the right word for it. It's almost like this... this mental wall? Like, I don't feel physically jittery, my skin isn't crawling, I don't feel like I need to run a mile or anything like that. It's completely tied to what's sitting on my computer screen. 

So, for example, I'll log in and open up my queue for the day, and I'll be scrolling through the claims I've been assigned. And if I see a file that I know is going to need a really long, detailed written explanation, or one where I’m going to have to dig in and check a bunch of really dense policy language to figure out if a specific procedure is covered... I just, I completely hit a wall. I will literally do anything to put it off. I'll look at it and tell myself, "Okay, I'll just knock out these quick, easy claims first, just to get the ball rolling and build some momentum." You know, the ones that just take a couple of clicks and you don't really have to think about them. 

But then I finish those, and I still can't bring myself to start the complex one. So I'll go hunt down more easy, quick tasks. I'll clear out my email inbox, I'll reorganize my digital folders, I'll do literally all the simple stuff until it's suddenly 4:30 in the afternoon and I'm basically out of time for the day anyway. 

And honestly, that moment when I realize I've run out of easy things to do and I absolutely *have* to look at that complicated file? That's usually the exact second I find myself standing up and walking to the printer or the breakroom. It's like my brain just absolutely refuses to do the heavy mental lifting, so it just hits the eject button and forces me to walk away from the desk entirely rather than sit there and read the policy.

symptom_reasoning.S006: The patient explicitly describes hitting a mental wall and doing anything to put off tasks that require dense reading or detailed explanations, referring to it as refusing to do 'heavy mental lifting.'
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient admits to standing up and walking away from their desk entirely when faced with a complicated task they want to avoid.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly denies feeling physically jittery, having crawling skin, or feeling the need to run.

turns.doctor_question: Outside of your work environment, do you find yourself frequently feeling the need to be on the go, or do you often interrupt others or finish their sentences before they are done speaking?
turns.patient_response:
Honestly, outside of work, I'm the complete opposite of "on the go." If you were to ask my girlfriend, she’d probably tell you I’m practically a couch potato. Like, just take this past weekend for example—we didn't have any major plans, and I was perfectly content to just sit on the sofa from, like, 10 AM until dinner time. I got completely sucked into this massive rabbit hole on YouTube watching these three-hour video essays about the history of defunct theme park rides, and I didn't feel any urge whatsoever to get up or go anywhere. Sometimes my friends will want to go out to a crowded bar downtown or go play pickup basketball, and I'm usually the one trying to talk them into just coming over and ordering a pizza so we don't have to leave the apartment. So, yeah, there's definitely no internal motor or anything driving me to be constantly moving when I'm off the clock. I'm totally fine just doing nothing. 

And as for the interrupting thing, or finishing people's sentences... no, I really don't think I do that either. If anything, it's kind of the other way around. When I'm in a conversation, especially if it's a group setting or if someone is telling a really long, drawn-out story about their day, I'm definitely not jumping in to talk over them. I'm usually just kind of... there. I'm usually trying really hard just to follow along with what they're saying, because my mind will inevitably start drifting off to whatever else I was thinking about earlier, like those theme park videos or a game I'm playing. 

So I'm definitely not finishing their sentences, because half the time, if I'm being completely honest, I've kind of lost the thread of what their sentence even started as. I'm way more likely to just nod and say "yeah, totally" when they pause, just hoping I didn't miss a direct question. I'm usually the quiet one in the group just trying to keep up, so I wouldn't say I'm jumping the gun or cutting people off at all.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient describes losing the thread of conversations and just nodding along, indicating difficulty listening when spoken to.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient mentions their mind inevitably drifting off to unrelated thoughts, such as videos or games, during conversations.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly denies feeling 'on the go' or having an internal motor driving them to be constantly moving.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly denies finishing other people's sentences.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient explicitly denies interrupting, talking over others, or cutting people off in conversations.
